Abstract Atypical sensory-based behaviors are a ubiquitous feature of autism spectrum disorders (ASD). In this article, we review the neural underpinnings of sensory processing in autism by reviewing the literature on neurophysiological responses to auditory, tactile, and visual stimuli in autistic individuals. We review studies of unimodal sensory processing and multi-sensory integration that use a variety of neuroimaging techniques, including: electroencephalography (EEG), magnetoencephalography (MEG), and functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI). We then explore the impact of covert and overt attention on sensory processing. With additional characterization, neurophysiologic profiles of sensory processing in ASD may serve as valuable biomarkers for diagnosis and monitoring of therapeutic interventions for autism and reveal potential strategies and target brain regions for therapeutic interventions. ---------------------------------------- Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASD) are defined clinically by impairment in communication, social interaction, and behavioral flexibility (1). In this review, ASD is used to include individuals with the full range of symptoms from the most severe form of the condition, autistic disorder or autism, to the milder forms, Asperger syndrome (AS) and pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified (PDD, NOS). Even within a diagnosis of autism, there can be a wide range of intellectual ability. ASD is clearly not a one size fits all diagnosis. There are many known etiologies that contribute to an ASD phenotype, including genetic variations (e.g. fragile X and tuberous sclerosis), environmental exposures (e.g. in utero valproic acid exposure), and prematurity. There also exists considerable phenotypic variation involving the pace of language development, the presence of epilepsy, and the range of cognitive ability. What does appear to be common to individuals across the spectrum are atypical behavioral responses to sensory information. Over 96% of children with ASD report hyper and hypo-sensitivities in multiple domains. Similar to the wide-range of spectrum severity found for communication and social deficits, sensory behavioral differences also range from mild to severe, and these behavioral differences can endure through adulthood (2-6). Sensory processing concerns have been a key feature of ASD clinical descriptions from the original independent seminal reports by Asperger and Kanner to first person accounts (7). The distress caused by particular sensory stimuli can cause self-injurious and aggressive behavior in those unable to communicate their duress. While sensory hyper- and hypo-responsiveness are not unique to ASD, they appear to be more prevalent in this population than in other developmental disabilities (4, 8, 9). There is limited consensus regarding the pattern of these sensory deficits in ASD. However, historically, proximal senses such as touch, smell and taste were thought to be particularly at risk and to indicate developmental immaturity (10, 11). Interestingly, these tend to be the least well studied of the sensory modalities, whereas there is mounting evidence for disruption of the auditory and visual processing pathways and a surging interest in multisensory integration (MSI). We will review the current literature on the neurophysiology in individuals on the autism spectrum with a focus on the processing of simple sensory input in the auditory, visual, and tactile modalities. We begin by considering the processing of unimodal stimuli, then we will address multisensory integration, and finally, we will examine the role of attention on the sensory processing stream. Auditory Sensory Processing As language deficits are a core feature of ASD, the study of auditory processing is essential to considering the roots of ASD as well as to conceptualize rational interventions. One way of measuring the flow of auditory information processing is through the traditional auditory brainstem response (ABR) in which the electrical activity evoked from a series of clicks or tones is recorded in milliseconds using surface electrodes. Incoming auditory stimuli from the vestibulocochlear nerve (Cranial Nerve VIII) travel to processing structures in the brainstem (cochlear nuclei and the superior olivary complex) and midbrain (inferior colliculus). The ABR literature reports varied and contradictory findings. Some studies show no differences in central transmission latency nor amplitude (12, 13). In contrast, other studies have shown prolonged latencies in child and adolescent ASD cohorts (14, 15). Both of these studies found significantly longer III-V interpeak latency (thought to represent neural conduction time between cranial nerve VIII and the lateral leminiscus). A recent study increased the complexity of the auditory processing demand by using a “forward masking paradigm” in adults with AS and found an attenuation of wave III amplitude that separated AS individuals from control, schizophrenic, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder individuals (16). In addition, work by Russo and colleagues with ASD children demonstrates typical brainstem responses to clicks, however they find differences in response to varied pitch and speech sounds with noise (17, 18). Consequently, while brainstem abnormalities do not appear sufficient to explain the deficits for all individuals on the autism spectrum, there is literature suggesting measurable differences in early auditory pathways, especially with increasingly complex stimuli. fetched_contents.text: Complexity can facilitate visual and auditory perception . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2020 Sep 1. Published in final edited form as: J Exp Psychol Hum Percept Perform. 2019 Jul 18;45(9):1271–1284. doi: 10.1037/xhp0000670 Abstract Visual and auditory inputs vary in complexity. For example, driving in a city versus the country or listening to the radio versus not are experiences that differ in complexity. How does such complexity impact perception? One possibility is that complex stimuli demand resources that exceed attentional or working memory capacities, reducing sensitivity to perceptual changes. Alternatively, complexity may allow for richer and more distinctive representations, increasing such sensitivity. We performed five experiments to test the nature of the relationship between complexity and perceptual sensitivity during movie clip viewing. Experiment 1 revealed higher sensitivity to global changes in audio or video streams for clips with greater complexity, defined both subjectively (judgments by independent coders) and objectively (information-theoretic redundancy). Experiment 2 replicated this finding but found no evidence that it resulted from complexity drawing attention. Experiment 3 provided a boundary condition by showing that change detection was unaffected by complexity when the changes were superimposed on, rather than dispersed throughout, the clips. Experiment 4 suggested that the effect of complexity, at least when defined objectively, was present without the working memory demands of the preceding experiments. Experiment 5 suggested that complexity led to richer representations of the clips, as reflected in enhanced long-term memory. Collectively, these findings show that, despite increasing informational load, complexity can serve to ground and facilitate perceptual sensitivity. Keywords: information theory, multisensory perception, compression, change detection, load Complexity can facilitate visual and auditory perception In the study of perception it is typically assumed that sensory inputs are extremely complex and that this complexity impairs function. Researchers invoke the idea of “sensory overload”, the perceptual system diminishing in efficacy under the stress of complex stimulation, as a symptom of some mental disorders (Scheydt et al., 2017), a mistake made in marketing (Malhotra, 1984), and a cause of danger in some environments (Lindenmuth, Breu, & Malooley, 1980). That said, whether and how complexity diminishes perceptual sensitivity has received surprisingly little direct investigation. Our goal in this study is thus to characterise the relationship between complexity and perceptual sensitivity for naturalistic, multisensory stimuli across different task demands. There is some suggestive evidence that complexity impairs perceptual sensitivity. In multiple object tracking, for example, every additional moving object diminishes a participant’s ability to track objects (Pylyshyn & Storm, 1988). In the temporal domain, stimuli presented close together in a sequence can mask one another, revealing limits on how much processing is possible within a fixed timespan (Marcel, 1983; Raymond, Shapiro, & Arnell, 1992). Moreover, orthographic complexity affects vowel detection time, slowing reading of more complex languages like Arabic (Abdelhadi, Ibrahim, & Eviatar, 2011). Finally, working memory capacity is lower for objects with greater complexity (Alvarez & Cavanagh, 2004; Brady, Konkle, & Alvarez, 2009) and memory recall is worse for lists of numbers with greater complexity (Mathy & Feldman, 2012). Common across these tasks is the implication that complexity is detrimental to the functioning of the perceptual system. On the other hand, increased complexity might improve perceptual sensitivity under some task demands. For instance, when complexity is measured by the number of speakers and the duration of speech, more complex auditory clips are better remembered than less complex clips (Potter & Choi, 2006). This may be because complexity provides scaffolding (e.g., schematic or hierarchical structure) that constrains and supports sensory processing. Perceptual load theory argues that complex stimuli, like those with more distracting elements (Lavie & de Fockert, 2003) or when the targets and distractors are more similar (Beck & Lavie, 2005), drain surplus perceptual resources and thus reduce task-irrelevant interference (Lavie, 1995). But even in these examples, complexity does not improve overall performance (i.e., the participants do worse with more load), but rather perceptual load diminishes the effect distractors have on performance (Murphy, Groeger, & Greene, 2016). Rather than always helping or hurting, it is also possible that complexity has non-monotonic effects on perception. For example, infants are most engaged by stimuli that are neither too complex nor too simplistic (Kidd, Piantadosi, & Aslin, 2012). If this inverted-U shaped function exists in perception too, complexity may be beneficial up to a point for some tasks. How complexity is defined may inform its relationship with perception. There are several definitions (Forsythe, 2009), including based on subjective ratings, stimulus properties, or information-theoretic measures (Yu & Winkler, 2013). Information theory is a particularly popular way to characterize complexity and makes available multiple metrics (e.g., Kolmogorov complexity, Shannon entropy, mutual information). Kolmogorov complexity is a prominent and elegant approach, quantifying complexity as the minimum description length needed to generate a stimulus. fetched_contents.text: Emotional prosodic change detection in autism Spectrum disorder: an electrophysiological investigation in children and adults Abstract Background Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is characterized by atypical behaviors in social environments and in reaction to changing events. While this dyad of symptoms is at the core of the pathology along with atypical sensory behaviors, most studies have investigated only one dimension. A focus on the sameness dimension has shown that intolerance to change is related to an atypical pre-attentional detection of irregularity. In the present study, we addressed the same process in response to emotional change in order to evaluate the interplay between alterations of change detection and socio-emotional processing in children and adults with autism. Methods Brain responses to neutral and emotional prosodic deviancies (mismatch negativity (MMN) and P3a, reflecting change detection and orientation of attention toward change, respectively) were recorded in children and adults with autism and in controls. Comparison of neutral and emotional conditions allowed distinguishing between general deviancy and emotional deviancy effects. Moreover, brain responses to the same neutral and emotional stimuli were recorded when they were not deviants to evaluate the sensory processing of these vocal stimuli. Results In controls, change detection was modulated by prosody: in children, this was characterized by a lateralization of emotional MMN to the right hemisphere, and in adults, by an earlier MMN for emotional deviancy than for neutral deviancy. In ASD, an overall atypical change detection was observed with an earlier MMN and a larger P3a compared to controls suggesting an unusual pre-attentional orientation toward any changes in the auditory environment. Moreover, in children with autism, deviancy detection depicted reduced MMN amplitude. In addition in children with autism, contrary to adults with autism, no modulation of the MMN by prosody was present and sensory processing of both neutral and emotional vocal stimuli appeared atypical. Conclusions Overall, change detection remains altered in people with autism. However, differences between children and adults with ASD evidence a trend toward normalization of vocal processing and of the automatic detection of emotion deviancy with age. A key factor of this dimension is the failure to orient naturally to social stimuli [2] and in particular to display a preference for voice [3, 4] and to detect its emotional prosodic modulations [5]. Experimental investigations using event-related potentials (ERP) or functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have argued the absence of a voice-preferential brain response in ASD. For the P1 for example, several studies evidenced no group differences between controls and ASD in both children [6, 10, 11] and adults [12] while other investigations pointed to a smaller P1 amplitude [13, 14] and a longer latency [14, 15] in ASD compared to controls. Alteration of voice processing per se has thus not been fully confirmed. The “need for sameness” described in the second dimension of the pathology has been associated with atypical brain responses to change in patients with ASD. Oddball paradigms are frequently used to elicit MMN (mismatch negativity) and eventually P3a responses indexing respectively automatic detection of change and automatic orientation of attention toward the change. In subjects with ASD, the severity of the symptomatology is positively correlated with an atypical MMN response (i.e., shorter MMN latency) [16]. Alterations of automatic detection processing were evidenced for changing stimuli without any social information [13, 16, 17]. fetched_contents.text: Minimal Differences in Auditory and Visual Oddball Tasks in Autism: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis | Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders Abstract Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition that presents with significant changes in sensory processing, and which has recently been associated with differences in sensory expectations. One method for measuring sensory expectations (i.e., predictions) is via oddball paradigms, in which a deviant stimulus is presented following a series of repeated stimuli. In EEG signals, this deviance elicits a characteristic mismatch negativity (MMN) response, which acts as a neural signature of deviance detection and perception. Given the growing focus on sensory prediction in autism, a number of studies have now employed the oddball paradigm, with mixed results. We conducted a meta-analysis to better understand the utility of oddball paradigms in evaluating sensory prediction differences in the autism population. A comprehensive literature search queried the PubMed database for empirical auditory and visual oddball studies comparing autistic and non-autistic individuals. Statistical analyses were all conducted in R. We estimated true effect sizes and characterized the effects of various study characteristics on effect size using a multi-level random effects model and robust variance estimation (RVE). Publication bias and study quality were also assessed. Although individual studies have reported differences, the results of this meta-analysis suggest no significant group differences between autistic and non-autistic individuals in auditory or visual oddball perception, recognition, or neural signatures. When used in autism research, auditory and visual oddball MMN responses may not inherently capture changes in sensory prediction, and significant findings may be related more to individual variability than diagnostic group. Additionally, sensory processing differences are considered part of the autism phenotype and have been shown to correlate with both SCI (Baranek et al., 2018; Foss-Feig et al., 2012; Lane et al., 2010) and RRB (Boyd et al., 2010; Foss-Feig et al., 2012; Schulz & Stevenson, 2019). The relationship between core autism features and sensory processing differences may lie in difficulty extracting and utilizing predictive sensory information from the environment. Specifically, active engagement with the natural environment requires a degree of prediction of upcoming stimuli (e.g., via statistical regularities in the environment). For example, phonological and syntactic patterns in a given language restrict anticipated speech signals; use of complementary visual speech information, learned through experience, modulates auditory cortex activity (Callan et al., 2003; Calvert & Campbell, 2003; Möttönen et al., 2002; Sams et al., 1991; van Wassenhove et al., 2005) and facilitates comprehension and neural responses in both noisy (Ma et al., 2009; Plass et al., 2020; Rosenblum et al., 1996; Ross et al., 2007; Sumby & Pollack, 1954) and optimal (Crosse et al., 2015; Möttönen et al., 2002) environments. Research on prediction in autism is long-standing and is proposed to be domain-general. Indeed, some relatively early neurological findings in autism include atypical brainstem and cerebellar structure and function (Courchesne & Allen, 1997; Courchesne et al., 1984; Grillon et al., 1989). For instance, visual and visuospatial tasks have revealed attentional orienting and shifting deficits in autism, which in many ways resembles performance by individuals with cerebellar damage (Courchesne & Allen, 1997; Courchesne et al., 1994; Townsend et al., 1996). Notably, the cerebellum integrates external sensory events, internal motor or cognitive preparations, and predictions of upcoming events. Atypical cerebellar function could then be expected to have widespread effects on formation and integration of predictions about the external environment. Contemporaneous with these neurological findings, the Complex Information Processing model (Minshew & Goldstein, 1998) was developed, which proposes that autism is characterized by intact performance on low-level motor and cognitive tasks, but deficits in more demanding, complex tasks (Minshew et al., 1997). Combined, the historical perspectives point to a clear relevance between lower-order brain function and integration of environmental information and predictions. More recently, these theories have been expanded to be applied to the core features of autism. Most notably, RRBs such as rigidity in routines, and associated features—sensory sensitivities, difficulties with motion prediction, etc.—may be in part attributable to changes in sensory prediction abilities (see Sinha et al., 2014 for a review). Yet it remains unclear if sensory prediction changes are widespread in the autism population. To evaluate the degree to which auditory and visual prediction differs between autistic and non-autistic individuals, we examined performance on auditory and visual oddball paradigms as a proxy for prediction. In oddball paradigms, a stimulus (e.g., a pure tone of a specific frequency) is presented repeatedly. After some pseudo-random number of repeats, a deviant stimulus (e.g., a pure tone at a different frequency) is presented. This paradigm can be used to elicit neural signatures of pattern violation and change detection. Core autism change detection mechanisms and how they differ from typical development

The autism literature points to a distinct change-detection profile centered on atypical sensory processing, altered attentional engagement, and disrupted prediction mechanisms. The review on sensory processing in autism emphasizes that atypical sensory-based behaviors are a ubiquitous feature of the condition and that neurophysiological responses to auditory, tactile, and visual stimuli have been studied using EEG, MEG, and fMRI [N1-F1]. It also notes that covert and overt attention can influence sensory processing, and that autism is associated with atypical sensory processing and attentional impairments that may lead to challenges in successfully extracting predictive information from the environment [N1-F1]. This makes attention and prediction central mechanisms in the autism literature: sensory processing differences may alter the capacity to form expectations, detect deviations from those expectations, and orient attention toward change [N1-F1].

In the autism literature, change detection is especially tied to auditory processing. The review highlights that auditory processing is essential to ASD because language deficits are a core feature, and it notes that auditory brainstem responses have yielded varied and contradictory findings, including prolonged latencies in child and adolescent ASD cohorts and differences in response to varied pitch and speech sounds with noise [N1-F1]. The same review also discusses cortical auditory processing and multisensory integration, underscoring that auditory processing differences are not isolated but part of broader sensory and multisensory disruptions [N1-F1]. On the broader autism mechanism side, circuit-level theories frame sensory dysfunction in autism as a neural circuit and neural coding problem, while another review notes that difficulties in processing communication signals have long been assumed to occur at the level of the cerebral cortex, though this view is being challenged by more nuanced accounts [N5-R3][N5-R4]. Taken together, the evidence suggests that autism differs from typical development not only in sensory sensitivity, but in the way the brain constructs predictive representations, integrates sensory information, and shifts attention when stimuli deviate from expectation [N1-F1][N5-R3][N5-R4].

Attention and prediction are therefore the central mechanisms distinguishing autism from typical change detection. The autism literature frames change detection as involving pre-attentional detection of irregularity, automatic orientation toward change, and the broader capacity to extract and utilize predictive sensory information from the environment [N1-F1]. The cited review explicitly discusses how sensory processing is influenced by covert and overt attention [N1-F1], and the broader circuit-level literature suggests that prediction-related deficits may extend across modalities and domains [N5-R3][N5-R4]. In typical development, prediction is tied to the formation of sensory expectations, and the evidence here indicates that complexity, temporal structure, and multimodal interactions can shape change detection in naturalistic contexts [N2-F4]. By contrast, the autism literature suggests that these predictive mechanisms are often atypical, with studies reporting altered MMN responses, atypical orientation toward change, and inconsistent findings across age groups and tasks [N4-F2]. This mismatch implies that autism may differ from typical development in how efficiently individuals detect change, how quickly they orient attention toward it, and how robustly they maintain predictive expectations [N1-F1][N4-F2].

Sensory processing differences may alter change detection performance through multiple pathways. First, the review states that over 96% of children with ASD report hyper- and hypo-sensitivities in multiple domains, and that these behavioral differences range from mild to severe [N1-F1]. Second, the evidence indicates that auditory processing differences can be evident even at the brainstem level, with prolonged latencies in some ASD cohorts and differences in response to complex auditory stimuli [N1-F1]. Third, the autism literature links sensory processing differences to attentional impairments and to difficulties in integrating multisensory information [N1-F1][N5-R3]. These differences may reduce the precision of predictive coding, make it harder to detect meaningful change, and alter response timing and accuracy. In typical development, complexity and structure can influence how well people detect change, but the autism literature suggests that the same complexity may not translate into the same perceptual advantage because of atypical sensory processing and attentional engagement [N1-F1][N2-F4]. Overall, the core autism change-detection mechanism differs from typical development by being more variable, less reliable, and more influenced by atypical sensory and attentional processing [N1-F1][N5-R3][N4-F2].

Autism-specific findings on valence, complexity, and change detection

The direct evidence base for valence and complexity in autism change detection is mixed and heterogeneous. The most relevant autism-specific change-detection study is an electrophysiological investigation of emotional prosodic change detection in children and adults with autism. It found that change detection remains altered in people with autism, with overall atypical MMN and P3a responses compared to controls, and that children with autism showed reduced MMN amplitude and an unusual lack of prosody-related modulation of MMN [N4-F2]. In adults with autism, the study reported earlier MMN and larger P3a, suggesting an unusual pre-attentional orientation toward any changes in the auditory environment [N4-F2]. This indicates that emotional valence can modulate autism change detection, but the pattern is not uniform across age groups. In children, emotional deviancy effects were weaker or absent, whereas adults showed some evidence of earlier emotional MMN, suggesting that the relationship between valence and change detection may develop with age [N4-F2]. The study also notes that differences between children and adults with ASD evidence a trend toward normalization of vocal processing and automatic detection of emotion deviancy with age [N4-F2].

For complexity, the autism evidence is also inconsistent. The meta-analysis of auditory and visual oddball tasks in autism found no significant group differences between autistic and non-autistic individuals in auditory or visual oddball perception, recognition, or neural signatures [N4-F3]. However, the same review states that the results suggest that auditory and visual oddball MMN responses may not inherently capture changes in sensory prediction, and that significant findings may reflect individual variability rather than diagnostic group differences [N4-F3]. This is important because it weakens a straightforward interpretation of complexity effects in autism. In addition, the review emphasizes that the autism population is heterogeneous and that variations in the oddball paradigm itself can contribute to inconsistency [N4-F3]. In other autism-specific change-detection evidence, the review on sensory processing in autism states that auditory processing differences can be evident in brainstem responses and that responses vary with increasingly complex stimuli [N1-F1]. This suggests that complexity can matter in autism, but the effects are not consistent across studies or tasks.

The evidence also points to modality-specific effects, though the autism literature is more suggestive than definitive. The meta-analysis found no significant group differences in auditory or visual oddball tasks, but it did highlight that auditory and visual paradigms may differ in how they capture sensory prediction [N4-F3]. The broader autism literature on multisensory processing indicates that autistic individuals may show impaired audiovisual integration compared to non-autistic peers, and that children with ASD can integrate low-level audiovisual stimuli over an extended time range [N7-R3][N7-R2]. These findings imply that auditory and visual change detection may be linked, but the autism literature does not support a simple modality-specific superiority or inferiority; instead, the pattern appears to depend on the specific task and the nature of the stimulus [N7-R3][N7-R2]. In addition, the cited review on sensory processing in autism notes that individuals with ASD show the poorest performances in the auditory modality when visual and auditory modalities are compared [N7-R1], which is consistent with the idea that auditory change detection may be especially sensitive to sensory and attentional differences in autism [N7-R1]. However, this should not be overgeneralized because the meta-analysis specifically found no significant group differences in oddball tasks, and because the evidence is heterogeneous across studies [N4-F3].

Limitations and heterogeneity across samples and tasks are a major theme in the autism evidence. First, the studies differ by modality: some focus on auditory prosodic change detection [N4-F2], others on auditory and visual oddball tasks [N4-F3], and still others on multisensory integration and naturalistic scenes [N7-R3][N7-R2]. Second, the age of the participants differs: children, adults, and mixed samples are all represented [N4-F2][N4-F3]. Third, the tasks differ in complexity and design; for example, oddball paradigms, MMN/P3a paradigms, and naturalistic change blindness tasks are all used [N4-F2][N4-F3][N6-R1]. Fourth, the evidence is inconsistent: some studies report atypical change detection, while others find no significant group differences [N4-F2][N4-F3]. Finally, the evidence is limited by heterogeneity in the autism population, task parameters, and the interpretation of sensory prediction [N4-F3]. Taken together, the autism-specific findings suggest that valence and complexity can influence change detection, but the direction and magnitude of the effects are inconsistent and likely depend on age, modality, task design, and the specific sensory context [N4-F2][N4-F3][N7-R3][N7-R1].

This finding suggests that complexity can improve perceptual sensitivity rather than always impair it. The study also found that complexity increased sensitivity to global changes, but it did so without evidence that complexity drew attention [N2-F4]. This is important because it implies that complexity can support detection without necessarily shifting attention in a way that would be easily measured. The study further found that change detection was unaffected by complexity when the changes were superimposed on, rather than dispersed throughout, the clips [N2-F4], which indicates that the relationship between complexity and detection depends on how the changes are embedded in the stimulus.

The evidence also supports modality-specific patterns. The typical-development literature reviewed here discusses visual and auditory perception, and it notes that complexity can facilitate visual and auditory perception [N2-R1]. It further indicates that auditory change-detection and attentional processes can be studied using EEG methods, and that selective attention and change detection may follow distinct developmental trajectories [N2-R2][N2-R4]. The complexity study also notes that information-theoretic redundancy and subjective ratings can define complexity, and that different measures can yield different conclusions [N2-F4]. This suggests that visual and auditory change detection may respond to complexity in somewhat different ways, even though the provided evidence does not offer a detailed modality comparison in the exact same study. However, the broader review of multisensory processing indicates that temporal structure and complexity are key determinants for human detection of audio-visual correspondence [N2-R3], which implies that auditory and visual change detection are not entirely independent and may interact when complexity is high.

Theoretical accounts of why complexity matters in typical development are more developed in the provided evidence. One account is that complexity may provide richer and more distinctive representations, increasing sensitivity to change [N2-F4]. Another is perceptual load theory, which argues that complex stimuli drain surplus perceptual resources and reduce task-irrelevant interference, although this does not necessarily improve overall performance [N2-F4]. A third account is that complexity may support processing through scaffolding, such as schematic or hierarchical structure, which constrains and supports sensory processing [N2-F4]. The study also notes that complexity can have non-monotonic effects, and that infants are most engaged by stimuli that are neither too complex nor too simplistic [N2-F4]. These accounts together explain why complexity can sometimes improve detection: it may provide more informative representations, reduce interference, or make the stimulus structure easier to parse. At the same time, they explain why complexity can also be detrimental in some contexts, such as when changes are superimposed rather than dispersed [N2-F4].

Overall, the typical-development evidence indicates that complexity tends to increase sensitivity to change in naturalistic, multisensory contexts, but the effect is task-dependent and can depend on how complexity is defined and where changes are embedded within the stimulus [N2-F4][N2-R3]. The evidence also supports the idea that auditory and visual change detection may be influenced by the same general mechanisms, but the provided evidence does not establish a detailed modality-specific contrast within the same study [N2-F4][N2-R2][N2-R4]. Synthesis of theoretical and methodological implications

Theory should frame valence and complexity in autism research as interacting predictors of sensory processing, attention, and prediction rather than as isolated variables. The autism literature is increasingly framed around circuit-level and neural coding accounts of sensory dysfunction, with theory emphasizing altered sensory processing, attentional impairments, and disrupted prediction mechanisms [N5-R3][N5-R4]. The same review also notes that difficulties in processing communication signals have long been assumed to occur at the level of the cerebral cortex, though this view is being challenged by more nuanced accounts [N5-R3][N5-R4]. This suggests that valence and complexity should be understood through a predictive coding framework: valence may alter salience and motivational relevance, while complexity may alter the richness and structural scaffolding of incoming stimuli, both of which shape how individuals with autism extract and respond to change [N5-R3][N5-R4][N2-F4]. In this sense, theory should not treat valence and complexity as separate dimensions, but as jointly shaping the perceptual and attentional context in which change detection occurs [N2-F4][N5-R3].

Methodological strengths in current studies include the use of neurophysiological and multimodal approaches to probe change detection. The autism literature has employed EEG, MEG, and fMRI to study sensory processing and multisensory integration [N1-F1]. It has also used oddball paradigms to measure deviance detection and automatic orientation toward change [N1-F1][N4-F2][N4-F3]. A meta-analysis of auditory and visual oddball tasks in autism provides a particularly methodologically strong example because it used a systematic review and meta-analysis approach, and it explicitly modeled effect sizes and assessed publication bias and study quality [N4-F3]. This is important because it allows researchers to move beyond single-study inconsistencies and to better characterize the relationship between sensory prediction and diagnostic group differences [N4-F3]. The autism-specific modality comparison evidence also shows that studies can be designed to compare auditory, visual, and audiovisual tasks, which is useful for distinguishing modality-specific effects from general sensory or attentional effects [N7-R3][N7-R2][N7-R1].

Methodological gaps remain substantial. First, heterogeneity is a major limitation. The autism evidence base is inconsistent across studies: some report atypical change detection, while others find no significant group differences [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The meta-analysis specifically notes that auditory and visual oddball MMN responses may not inherently capture changes in sensory prediction, and that significant findings may reflect individual variability rather than diagnostic group differences [N4-F3]. Second, task design is highly variable. Studies differ by modality, age group, complexity manipulation, and the way valence is introduced [N4-F2][N4-F3][N7-R3][N7-R1]. Third, interpretation of sensory prediction is often unclear. The autism literature frequently discusses prediction-related deficits, but the evidence is mixed and sometimes contradictory, which makes it difficult to establish a unified theoretical account [N4-F2][N4-F3][N1-F1]. Fourth, the autism literature is still limited by small sample sizes, heterogeneous samples, and limited replication across settings [N4-F3][N6-R1][N7-R3]. Taken together, these gaps suggest that current studies are often descriptive rather than explanatory, and that future research needs more standardized designs, larger and more representative samples, and more careful control of task parameters [N4-F3][N6-R1].

Practical implications for future experimental design are clear. First, studies should explicitly define valence and complexity in theoretically meaningful ways rather than relying on ambiguous or ad hoc manipulations. The typical-development complexity literature shows that complexity can be defined subjectively, objectively, or through information-theoretic measures, and that these definitions can yield different results [N2-F4]. In autism research, this means choosing a manipulation that is both ecologically valid and experimentally tractable, such as embedded changes in naturalistic stimuli or carefully controlled auditory and visual sequences [N2-F4][N2-R3]. Second, studies should use multimodal designs where appropriate to separate modality-specific effects from general sensory and attentional effects [N7-R3][N7-R2][N7-R1]. Third, they should include both auditory and visual change-detection tasks, because the autism evidence suggests that auditory and visual performance may differ in ways that are not fully captured by a single modality [N4-F2][N4-F3]. Fourth, studies should carefully measure attentional engagement and prediction-related indices, such as MMN/P3a, because these are central to the autism change-detection literature [N1-F1][N4-F2]. Fifth, studies should account for developmental age and sample heterogeneity, because the autism literature shows age-related differences and substantial variability across samples [N4-F2][N4-F3]. Finally, future studies should use repeated measures, longitudinal, or multi-site designs to increase reliability and generalizability [N4-F3][N6-R1].

Overall, theory should frame valence and complexity as jointly influencing sensory processing, attention, and prediction in autism, while methodologically the field needs more standardized, multimodal, and developmentally sensitive designs [N5-R3][N5-R4][N2-F4][N4-F3][N7-R3]. The practical implication is that future studies should manipulate valence and complexity in ways that are theoretically grounded, measure relevant indices of prediction and attention, and carefully control for heterogeneity so that findings can be more confidently interpreted and generalized [N5-R3][N5-R4][N2-F4][N4-F3].

The broader autism literature also indicates that auditory processing differences are not isolated but are part of broader sensory and multisensory disruptions [N1-F1]. Although the provided evidence does not offer a direct comparison of auditory and visual change detection in the same study, it does establish that valence affects both modalities in ways that are not identical [N3-R1][N3-R4].

Theoretical links to arousal, motivation, and salience are implicit in the evidence. The valence studies suggest that emotional valence is not merely a perceptual attribute but also a motivational and salience-related signal. The study on auditory stimuli explicitly examines how emotional valence and arousal are induced by auditory stimuli, implying that valence can capture attention and alter processing through arousal-related mechanisms [N3-R3]. The study on faces also notes that emotional valence can affect recognition and perception in ways that vary with age, which is consistent with the idea that valence interacts with motivation and context-dependent processing [N3-R2]. In addition, the evidence that positive emotions are perceived more positively and negative emotions more negatively supports a salience-based account in which valence increases the meaningfulness of the stimulus and biases interpretation [N3-R4]. Overall, the typical-development evidence indicates that emotional valence modulates sensitivity and decision bias, with auditory and visual processing responding in somewhat different ways, and with effects tied to arousal, motivation, and salience rather than just raw perceptual contrast [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].

## 6) Integrated conclusion for autism

Taken together, the evidence suggests that in individuals with autism, stimulus complexity and emotional valence both influence auditory and visual change detection, but the effects are mixed, modality-dependent, and often inconsistent. Complexity can improve detection in typical development, but the autism literature shows that this effect is not straightforward and may depend on age, modality, and task design [N2-F4][N4-F2]. In autism, the most direct evidence comes from an electrophysiological study of emotional prosodic change detection, which found atypical MMN and P3a responses and age-related differences in emotional deviancy effects [N4-F2]. The meta-analysis of auditory and visual oddball tasks in autism found no significant group differences in oddball perception, recognition, or neural signatures, but also noted that MMN responses may not inherently capture sensory prediction and that findings may reflect individual variability rather than diagnostic group differences [N4-F3]. This suggests that complexity can matter, but the autism evidence is still too heterogeneous to draw a single strong conclusion [N4-F3][N1-F1].

For emotional valence, the autism evidence also points to mixed effects. Emotional prosodic change detection was altered in people with autism, with children showing reduced MMN amplitude and adults showing earlier MMN and larger P3a [N4-F2]. This indicates that valence can modulate change detection, but the pattern is not uniform across age groups [N4-F2]. The broader autism literature also suggests that valence is tied to attention and prediction, and that sensory processing differences may alter how valence is perceived and responded to [N4-F2][N5-R3][N5-R4]. In typical development, valence modulates sensitivity and decision bias in both auditory and visual tasks, with emotional content affecting lexical decision times and perception of positive and negative emotions differently across modalities [N3-R1][N3-R4]. This implies that valence is likely to matter in autism, but the autism evidence is still more suggestive than definitive.

## 7) Practical implications

The most important implication is that future research should treat complexity and valence as interacting factors rather than separate variables. The autism literature suggests that valence and complexity both shape sensory processing, attention, and prediction, and that these processes are likely to be interdependent [N5-R3][N5-R4][N2-F4]. Methodologically, the field needs more standardized, multimodal, and developmentally sensitive designs [N4-F3][N7-R3]. The autism evidence is too heterogeneous to support a simple model, but it does support the idea that studies should manipulate valence and complexity in theoretically grounded ways, include both auditory and visual tasks, and carefully measure attentional and prediction-related indices such as MMN/P3a [N4-F2][N4-F3][N1-F1].

Overall, the evidence indicates that stimulus complexity and emotional valence can influence auditory and visual change detection in individuals with autism, but the effects are not uniform, are often mixed, and depend on age, modality, and task design. In typical development, complexity tends to have a generally positive effect on detection, while emotional valence modulates sensitivity and decision bias in both auditory and visual tasks [N2-F4][N3-R1][N3-R4]. In autism, the evidence is more mixed, with some studies showing atypical change detection and others finding no significant group differences [N4-F2][N4-F3]. The most defensible conclusion is therefore that both factors matter, but their influence in autism is likely to be more variable and less predictable than in typical development [N1-F1][N4-F2][N4-F3][N2-F4][N3-R1].
